samples.hyp: Assessing the necessary levels of SARS-CoV-2 testing to control the outbreak in Lusaka province, Zambia, considering asymptomatic individuals:
A simple statistical study.

The novel Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome—2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa is characterized by a very high number of people who are asymptomatic (or have mild symptoms) who are thought to play an asymptomatic role in the spread of the disease.
The proportion and exact rate of infection among asymptomatic individuals remain unclear.
However, the study indicates that their management is crucial in controlling the transmission of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a simplified deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) mathematical model to assess the impact of effective isolation of asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals through blanket testing to control the outbreak in Lusaka Province, Zambia.
Here we estimate two scenarios; (1) assuming that asymptomatic individuals account for 70% of all COVID-19 cases and (2) asymptomatic individuals account for only 50% of the cases.

Conversely, the model was initially tested under the assumption that asymptomatic individuals are equally infectious as symptomatic individuals and secondly, and possibly, it was assumed that asymptomatic individuals have half the infections as symptomatic individuals.

In a model assuming 70% asymptomatic cases, a minimum ongoing rate of daily blanket testing of ≥ 7911 tests per 100,000 population would be sufficient to control an outbreak if asymptomatic individuals were only a portion of the infections, whereas if equal infection was assumed, a testing rate of ≥ 10028 tests per 100,000 population would be required.

In 50% of asymptomatic cases, low testing rates of ≥ 4540/ per 100000 population are insufficient to control outbreaks at both assumed infection rates in asymptomatic individuals related to symptomatic individuals.
Discussion and conclusion

Our model predicts that effective isolation of COVID-19 cases, including asymptomatic individuals, through blanket testing can be used as a measure to control the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but it will come at a high cost.
Testing in large cities like Lusaka could limit the spread of COVID-19, but is it effective?
In 2020, computer models predicted that the spread of COVID-19 in major cities could be better controlled by testing a large number of people, and then isolating all those who tested positive.
However, researchers say this method may be expensive and ineffective.
At the beginning of the pandemic, many people who were infected with COVID-19 did not show symptoms of the disease and spread it to others.
Another study suggested that 50 to 80% of people with COVID-19 were asymptomatic and may be responsible for 40 to 70% of new infections.
Researchers wanted to know if identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help control the spread of COVID-19.
They also want to know whether mass testing, meaning testing a large number of people randomly, successfully identifies asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers developed a computer model that predicts how people progress through exposure, infection, and isolation.
They focused on information from the province of Lusaka in Zambia, which is a business hub with an international airport located at the border of two countries.

Because the characteristics of COVID-19 appeared to vary by region, they considered 4 scenarios, where either 50% or 70% of COVID-19 cases were asymptomatic, and these cases were equally or half as transmissible as those with symptoms.
The researchers' model found that it is possible to control the spread of COVID-19 by conducting blanket testing and isolating all individuals who test positive, even those who are asymptomatic.
To reduce the maximum number of cases by 90% in all scenarios, 10% of the people in Lusaka need to be tested daily.
They also found that if we want to keep the number of new people infected with COVID-19 unchanged, 22% of people need to be tested daily.
Although Zambia implemented numerous measures to curb COVID-19, cases appeared to be increasing.
The testing of the garment successfully reduced the number of COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small town in Italy.
However, there are no previous studies suggesting that it will work well in a large city elsewhere.
Note that the researchers did not conduct garment testing in this study; instead, they developed a model suggesting that garment testing could work to reduce the spread of COVID-19 in large cities.
However, they warned that it is likely to be very expensive.
They further stated that it may be more effective when combined with other methods, such as lockdowns, contact tracing, and vaccination.
Researchers in Zambia further emphasized that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases appeared to be very common in Africa at that time.
The low normalization of genetic points in African people is due to genetic and environmental diversity.
The statistics of African people are significantly underrepresented in genetic studies but have a high genetic diversity and face extensive environmental exposure globally.

Due to the lack of systematic testing of genetic predictions in ancestors encompassing African diversity, we calculated polygenic risk scores (PRS) in simulations across Africa and in a collection of evidence from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to better understand the generalizability of genetic studies.
The accuracy of PRS improves with ancestry-matched discovery cohorts over those from non-ancestry-matched studies.
For South Africans of diverse ancestries and ethnicities, we find that the accuracy of the PRS is low across all traits but varies among groups.
The difference in African ancestry has a significant impact on the variation in PRS accuracy compared to another major group difference hypothesized between people in the UK when compared to Uganda.

We constructed a PRS computer for African individuals using only existing European genetic studies compared to ancient ones; the increased diversity produced significantly greater accuracy benefits for hemoglobin concentration and white blood cell count, indicating enriched ancestral diversity in genetic loci known to influence sickle cell anemia and inflammatory responses, respectively.
The difference in the accuracy of PRS among all African ancestors from different regions is as large as among all non-African ancestors, requiring comparable diversity.
Why can't we accurately predict genetic diseases in indigenous African populations?
Researchers say that the current methods used to predict whether a person will have a genetic disease or not do not work well for indigenous African people.
This is because the database that follows these predictions generally describes the genetic characteristics of people of European descent.
The GWAS database stands for "Genome-Wide Association Studies", and scientists use it to investigate genetic traits and diseases.
In fact, they can use GWAS to calculate an individual's genetic risk for a disease or trait.
Most of the genetic data in GWAS, however, comes from individuals of European ancestry.
In this study, researchers aimed to determine whether the statistics they use to assess the risk of genetic diseases using GWAS are applicable to indigenous African populations.
They also wanted to see if a more diverse GWAS, in other words, a database that includes additional African genetic information, could improve predictions.
The number is scientifically known as "Polygenic Risk Scores", or PRS.

They use computers to calculate the predicted genetic risks for African people using GWAS, and they use medical records of African people to examine certain traits or diseases that may be caused by genetic variations.
When using the European GWAS, they found that genetic risk scores were more accurate when individuals were of European descent compared to those of African descent for many traits.
They said the risk levels are much lower among African regions because there is a diversity of people, which is not consistent with what we see among the indigenous people of Europe.
They further stated that the accuracy of PRS increases as African ancestry decreases.
People in Ethiopia had better predictions for genetic diseases as they are more genetically similar to people in Europe.
When using a diverse GWAS that includes people of African descent, the prediction accuracy improved.
The prediction of blood diseases was very accurate.
Previous research has shown that the PRS is low in African populations, indicating that the GWAS database predicts a lower risk of genetic diseases in African people.
However, we know that this is not really true.

This study explains that the low risk statistics for genetic diseases are due to the underrepresentation of African genetic variants in the GWAS database, therefore the current PRS values are not really helpful in predicting genetic diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be better to use a diverse database that includes genetic information from African people.
Therefore, another effort is needed to diversify GWAS to include African ancestry so that we can accurately predict the genetic disease risk in African populations.
The authors of this study were from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
Visual Inspection and Cytology Screening in the Prevention of Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
Approximately 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of infection with the human papilloma virus (HPV) which could cause cervical cancer.
Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy have been evaluated for their effectiveness.
However, information associated with the impact of cervical cancer screening programs is lacking.
This study examined visual inspection and cytology testing in the prevention of cervical intraepithelial lesions (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.
Findings showed that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at an increased risk of testing positive for VIA.
Older women, particularly those with HIV, are more likely to be diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
The VIA procedure appears to be effective in screening, although follow-up colposcopy in the Namibian context should be reviewed and utilized with positive HR-HPV results.
Testing methods that include screening for HPV at different ages and the number of people at risk (e.g., having HIV, autoimmune disease) are recommended.

The use of testing can be continuously improved through interventions that utilize a model employing previous diagnostic outcomes, women's health objectives, recent knowledge, and appropriate actions in the national context.
Women in Namibia who are at risk of cervical cancer should be screened and treated early.
Further testing can indicate the risk of cervical cancer in women, but regular screening in Namibia does not always use this testing.
Researchers suggested regular screening, to detect early warning signs, which could prevent women from developing this deadly disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the lower part of the uterus) causes the death of many women worldwide.
One of the most common causes of cervical cancer is the Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that damages the cervix, creating lesions that can eventually lead to cancer.
Although the HPV vaccine is available, many women in African countries, including Namibia, cannot access it.
This means that testing for the virus or the lesions it causes is very important for these women, as it is the best way to help prevent cancer.
Researchers in this study say that hospitals therefore need appropriate guidelines and information about the best tests to be used.
They added that healthcare workers need more information about how factors such as age or health affect a woman's risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
They investigated how some common types of tests (referred to as screening methods) were used to detect HPV and lesions.
They also showed interest in comparing testing methods, for example, collecting cervical cells to examine damage as opposed to just observing lesions.
They also wanted to know whether differences among women, such as their age, or whether they have other diseases like HIV, altered the chances of acquiring HPV and cancer.
Knowing this information can help hospitals and clinics to implement effective screening methods.
Researchers examined the medical records of 214 women who were tested and treated for HPV, lesions, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
They focused heavily on early-stage cervical cancer, where the disease can be treated easily and successfully.
They also collected information about each woman's age, as well as her overall health.

By reviewing these records, they found that different testing methods generally provide healthcare workers with distinct information, and that they can be very useful before or after HPV develops into cancer.
Cancer, for example, was commonly detected by collecting and examining cervical cells.
Ulcers, however, were commonly detected through visual examination, using a method called "visual inspection with acetic acid" (VIA).
The advantage of this procedure is that it allows doctors to detect lesions quickly at a low cost.
This is because it uses basic medical equipment already used for examining women's diseases, such as a speculum (an instrument used to look inside the vagina).
They also found that combining different methods often provides doctors with additional information about a woman's risk of developing cancer, especially through frequent testing.
Moreover, researchers found that older women, particularly those with HIV, are more likely to be diagnosed with cancer, thus regular screening can be very important for them.
Researchers further added that very few women are tested for HPV (before examining lesions) even though testing is available.
Doing so could be an important way to detect this disease quickly.

Overall, they stated that their results indicate a need for the health system in Namibia to strategically plan HPV and cervical cancer prevention methods, using affordable and effective screening techniques to detect these diseases early.
This study was a collaboration between scientists from Namibia and South Africa.
The benefit of simultaneous treatment of HBV/HIV co-infection compared to HBV infection alone in a South African cohort.

Driven by global goals to eliminate the hepatitis B virus (HBV), we aim to distinguish individuals with HBV alone compared to those co-infected with both HBV and HIV simultaneously, to analyze the impact of treatment and control progress in healthcare management.
We report findings from a real-world mixed cohort of 115 adults with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) infection, at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
HIV co-infection and another disease were present in 39 (34%) of the study participants.
We recorded mixed demographic health data from the laboratory.

Compared to those with HIV coinfection, older individuals with HBV monoinfection were less likely to be HBeAg-positive (p=0.01), less likely to have undergone elastography (p<0.0001), and less likely to have received antiviral treatment (p<0.0001); they were more likely to have HBV viraemia (p=0.04), and more likely to have liver disease features including moderate/severe thrombocytopaenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and a higher APRI score (p=0.02).
Three cases of hepatocellular carcinoma all arose from infection with HBV alone.
Our data indicates that individuals with HBV alone may be disadvantaged compared to those with HIV and another disease, highlighting the disparity in reporting, monitoring, and treatment.
Researchers provide guidelines to improve the treatment of hepatitis B.
In a recent study, researchers were able to clarify that co-infection with both hepatitis B (HBV) and HIV can provide treatment benefits beyond infection with HBV alone.
In Southern Africa, co-infection with both HBV and HIV is a major problem.
Doctors need to understand how these viruses and the medications used to treat them interact, so that they can better diagnose diseases and care for patients.
Researchers wanted to compare the treatment outcomes in patients with HBV only, and patients with both HBV and HIV.
In this study, researchers recruited 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were gathered at Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients were infected with HIV (39) while others were infected with HBV only.
Researchers examined skin color, age, and gender, and then conducted several health and laboratory tests.
They found that patients with HBV alone were less likely to receive treatment, indicating the natural disease progression of liver disease (as HBV is a virus that can lead to severe liver disease).

Researchers were able to demonstrate that individuals with only HBV were disadvantaged compared to those with both HIV and HBV, as patients infected with both viruses had the opportunity to receive HIV treatment, which provides a certain benefit in combating HBV infection.

The results from this study clarify the potential impact of differences between reporting, monitoring, and treatment options for HBV when compared to the management of HIV and HBV simultaneously, favoring those affected by both HIV and HBV.
Researchers emphasize that we must improve and provide safe and unbiased assistance to patients with HBV only.
One limitation of this study is the small number of participants that were specific to one country and its hospital systems.
Some, perhaps a few hospital systems may show contradictory findings compared to what this study found.
Further studies may be needed to better understand the differences found in this study.
This paper demonstrated the power of collaboration, with researchers working on this project in South Africa and the United Kingdom.
Using patients from South Africa in this study, it pertains to the segment of the African population.
Moreover, the study can help develop better treatment programs for those affected by HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessment of the Impact of Insecurity on Women's Business Activities in the SHIRORO Local Government Area of Niger State.

This study examined the impact of insecurity on the business activities of women in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing particularly on issues related to women's financial dependency, the types of business activities common among them, and the extent of the impact of insecurity on their businesses.
A sample of 377 women was examined, leading to the finding that women in Shiroro are entrepreneurs with a high level of financial independence, and are heavily involved in SMEs.

The study also found that although insecurity has a negative impact on women's business activities in terms of loss or decline in finances among other things, the number of women entrepreneurs did not experience a significant decrease.

The study recommended that sustainable programs to improve women's access to and use of financial services should be created, and public policing organizations should also be established and strengthened to combat insecurity in the study area.
Women entrepreneurs in Niger need additional protection.
Researchers found that female entrepreneurs in Niger are businesspeople and financially independent, but security from criminals is a concern.

Researchers wanted to know how safe and secure women running businesses in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State are, and what impact this might have on their businesses and financial independence.
They interviewed 377 women from the area about the challenges they face regarding their business, financial dependency, and insecurity.
They reported that 43% of women said they do not rely on men for money, while 32% said they have other people they depend on for money.
Researchers also found that 85% of women earn money through various businesses, with few stating that they rely on salaries.
About 56% made money through farming, and 79% made money through trading.
About 1 in 5 women earned money by braiding hair, sewing, knitting, or washing.
The majority of women (91%) told researchers that their businesses were affected due to fear of attacks by thieves and criminals.
They lose money, even their husbands, due to these attacks, sometimes forcing them to raise their children alone.
These women also stated that they do not have the skills and sufficient funds to grow their businesses.
Researchers reported that despite these challenges, women in Niger continued to perform very well in their businesses.
They said Shiroro has people of different ethnicities and religions, and this also helps in businesses.
This study challenges the findings of other researchers who reported that women have less success in business because they are caregivers at home.
Instead, these researchers say the success of businesswomen in this area of Niger is greatly affected by the threat of attacks by criminals and thieves.
Researchers recommend that all stakeholders should come together to combat factors that can hinder success in business.
For example, women in Niger should have increased access to finance, farms, and security.
They also suggested that women in businesses can form groups to help them fight against thieves and criminals.
Maternal Serum Concentrations of Selenium, Copper, and Zinc During Pregnancy Are Associated With the Risk of Spontaneous Preterm Birth: A Case-Control Study From Malawi
Discussing preterm birth, which occurs before completing 37 weeks.
The study was conducted to investigate the relationship between the severity of selenium, copper, and zinc in the serum of mothers, and preterm birth.
There were 181 women in this study where the individual was known by name. 90/181 (49.7%) reached menstruation while 91/181 (50.3%) conceived before menstruation.

The mean concentration of serum selenium was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, copper was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and zinc was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L with reference ranges of 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
The results indicate that there was no deficiency of selenium, as well as zinc and elevated serum lead levels during pregnancy.
Preterm birth is associated with high levels of copper and zinc in the serum of mothers.
The deficiency of zinc, copper, and selenium is associated with premature birth.
Researchers found elevated levels of trace nutrients selenium, copper, and zinc in women who experience premature labor, but they do not know if these elevated levels originate from their diet.
Preterm labor occurs when a woman goes into labor before 37 weeks of pregnancy.
Preterm birth is associated with negative health outcomes for the child from aspects of development to mortality.
There can be many causes of premature birth, but the role of high levels of micronutrients that are rarely needed, found in food and the environment, is not well known.
These nutrients, which are needed in small amounts, are essential for a child's growth, but researchers want to know what happens when they are present in excess.

In this study, researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who gave birth prematurely, and then identify the likelihood that premature birth is caused by high levels of each of these nutrients studied.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women shortly after they gave birth at two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital of Malawi, between June 2016 and March 2017.
They transported blood samples to a laboratory in Norway where they extracted serum, a clearer state of blood, and then measured the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.
About half of the women in the study gave birth prematurely and researchers found very high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.

They adjusted their statistics to account for other factors such as age, general health status, and pregnancy history in order to isolate the suspected effects of these nutrients that are minimally required in causing preterm birth.
They concluded that high levels of selenium and copper did not play a visible role in causing premature birth, but that high levels of zinc increased the risk of premature birth by more than 6 times.
High levels of mercury have caused concern among researchers, due to its known toxic effects.

Having only 181 women participating in the study limited the researchers' ability to accurately identify the risks associated with high levels of selenium, as the appropriate number of participants is 600.
The daily diet of the participants was not investigated to identify potential sources of these micronutrients, and their Body Mass Index (BMI) was not recorded.
This is the first study of its kind measuring the effects of selenium, copper, and zinc in pregnant women in Malawi.
Africa has one of the highest rates of preterm births - over 18% compared to 5% in Western countries, so researchers want to know if nutrition has an impact.
Domestic Behavior, Site Fidelity, and Habitat of the Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals exhibit unique spatial and temporal behaviors that enhance their survival.
Understanding such behavior is a crucial step in the successful conservation and management, especially of endangered animals.

In this study, we examined whether the Pancake tortoise was resilient when relocated and investigated the habitat fidelity and the range of species residing in natural habitats in Kitui County, Kenya.

The behavior of 39 tortoises residing in 12 isolated rock crevices was studied from July 2020 to June 2022 using radio tracking, camera setup, and a combination of group-level scan sampling and ad libitum sampling.
Fourteen tortoises were fitted with radio transmitters and were relocated from their burrows to other burrows far from their home burrows, and their movements and behavior were monitored.

Except for only two females that adapted well to new migration routes, all other turtles attempted to return home, with 46.15% of them accurately retracing their path back to their home routes and 15.38% also reaching areas believed to be within their home.
Success at home provides strong evidence of site reliability in the species.

The analysis of turtle burrow occupancy showed that there was no statistically significant difference in the number of turtles initially present in burrows with an average number present during the 162 sample days (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P >0.05), continuously supporting the strong site fidelity in the species.
On the other hand, camera trapping events and ad libitum sampling further demonstrated that Pancake tortoises are territorial with males defending their areas aggressively against intruding males.
Lost pancake tortoises have an unusual ability to 'find home'

Researchers discovered something surprising while studying the behavior of pancake tortoises in East Africa (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals can find their way back home after being transported long distances.
Understanding how they do this and why they are important in the conservation of these rare reptiles.
The way these turtles are shown to find homes is called "homing," and many other animals can do that.
The ability to return to specific locations allows animals to revisit food sources, territories, and habitats, enhancing their chances of survival and reproduction.

Although domestic behavior has been studied in sea turtles and freshwater environments, researchers in this study say there is still very little we know about living in turtle habitats (areas equivalent to turtles).
In this study, researchers aim to gain a deeper understanding of the behavior of pancake tortoises in their natural habitat in the rocky areas of Kenya.
They study the animals as they move and feed, and where they rest in crevices, or gaps in the rock.
Researchers observed groups of tortoises for about two years, and set up cameras to record video of the animals when they were not being watched.
They also attached radio transmitters to 14 turtles.
These small tools allow researchers to track the movement of animals, and monitor where they spend their time during the day and night.
The researchers then relocated some of these tracked tortoises to a new location, so they could study them more easily.
However, to the researchers' surprise, two turtles began returning to their original locations, between 1 and 2.5 kilometers from where they had been removed.
It was at that time that researchers decided to try to remove many animals away from their homes, to see if they would exhibit the same 'homing' behavior.
I used to live before they were relocated, often traveling more than 1.5 km to get there.
Another 15% of them were able to return to the usual location, but they did not find the gap from which it was initially taken.
Researchers also found that different crevices generally have the same number of turtles resting in them, suggesting that turtles consistently use the same resting spots.
Images from the cameras also showed that male tortoises were territorial, meaning they fought with other males trying to enter their territory or burrows.

Researchers say it is the first time that homing behavior has been observed in pancake tortoises, and their findings indicate that these animals prefer to stay and rest in the same locations whenever they can.
Their study did not describe how the turtles found their way home, so future research should focus on understanding this important point.
Because animals sometimes need to be relocated to new areas for conservation, this information will help conservationists keep tortoises safe in their new environment.
This study was a collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, and it adds to our knowledge of the behavior of turtles and other animals.
The Plasma Pharmacokinetics of high oral dose compared to Intravenous Rifampicin in patients with tuberculous meningitis:
Randomized controlled trial
A high dose of intravenous rifampicin may improve the outcomes of tuberculosis meningitis but is not prepared for use in high-burden settings.

It is hypothesized that plasma rifampicin levels will be similar between an oral dose of 35mg/kg body weight and an intravenous dose of 20mg/kg, which is proposed to be tested for efficacy in tuberculosis meningitis.
We conducted a randomized parallel-group pharmacokinetic study embedded within a clinical trial of intensified antimicrobial treatment for tuberculous meningitis.
Participants with HIV and tuberculosis meningitis were identified in South African hospitals and were placed into one of three rifampicin dosage groups:
standard (oral 10mg/kg), high dose (oral 35mg/kg), and intravenous (20mg/kg).
A large pharmacokinetic sample was taken on day 3.
The information was described using noncompartmental analysis, exposure was compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants provided pharmacokinetic samples (standard dose, n= 17; high oral dose, n= 15; intravenous, n= 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The geometric mean area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0–24) values for rifampicin were 42.9mg · h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0mg · h/ml) for the standard dose, 295.2mg · h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8mg · h/ml) for the high oral dose, and 206.5mg · h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8mg · h/ml) for intravenous administration.

The rifampicin AUC0–24 GMR was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21) with the maximum drug concentration in serum (Cmax) GMR being 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) when administered as a high oral dose compared to intravenous infusion.
The plasma rifampicin AUC0–24 was higher after an oral dose of 35 mg/kg than with intravenous administration of 20 mg/kg during the first few days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The findings support the oral dosage of rifampicin in future evaluations of tuberculous meningitis.
High-dose pills can be tested in patients with HIV and brain TB.
Researchers have confirmed that it is appropriate to begin investigating whether higher doses of the drug rifampicin can save patients with HIV and tuberculous meningitis.
Three out of every five patients with HIV who also contract tuberculous meningitis die from this disease, which attacks the nervous system.
Survivors are often left with permanent damage to their central nervous system and critical nerves emanating from the brain.
This can affect their emotions and movements.
Some patients experience seizures or strokes, or parts of their face or body become paralyzed.
Rifampicin, a powerful drug used against tuberculosis, is commonly administered as tablets to attempt to kill the bacteria causing tuberculous meningitis.
Patients who are severely ill often find it difficult to swallow pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered by injection (intravenously) in liquid form.
Then a needle is inserted into the patient's veins to remove fluid from the body.
No tests have been conducted to determine how the patient's body absorbs the medication when this method is used.
Injection treatment requires numerous tools, hospitalization, and a trained healthcare professional capable of administering the needle into the vein correctly.
Therefore, it is not a method to be used in regions of the world that lack all resources.
Doctors now know that rifampicin is not well absorbed into the cerebrospinal fluid, the spine, and the brain, which is where bacteria can hide.
This is why high doses (amounts) are necessary to effectively kill all the bacteria in the patient's body.
However, researchers were uncertain about how effective and safe a higher dose could be.

Therefore, researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom wanted to determine, using a small number of patients, whether it is safe to administer high doses of rifampicin as pills or by injection, and how their bodies would absorb each form.
It is important to know this before other researchers begin large trials, or studies, where they plan to give many patients high doses of rifampicin.
One of the three treatment regimens of rifampicin was given to 46 South African patients with HIV and tuberculous meningitis.
The first was the standard treatment of pills currently given to patients, which includes 10mg of rifampicin per kilogram of the patient's weight.
Another group received tablets with a high dose of 35 milligrams per kilogram of the patient's body weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram by body weight intravenously.
Blood samples were taken from patients after three days.
The researchers then measured the amount of rifampicin present in their blood plasma (the liquid component of blood).
Higher levels of rifampicin were found in the bodies of patients who received high-dose tablets compared to those who received treatment by injection or the standard dose.
The concentration of the drug in the blood plasma was similar to that of a high dose and treatment by injection.
This concentration was higher than when patients received only the standard dose.
According to researchers, this suggests that the health of patients with tuberculous meningitis can improve if they receive higher doses of rifampicin.
It does not matter whether they receive it as pills or intravenously - what is important is that they receive high doses, because their bodies are able to maintain its high concentration.
The results support the findings of trials conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
Two small trials in Indonesia, for example, suggested that the lives of many patients could be saved if they are given high doses of rifampicin orally or intravenously.
Unfortunately, however, researchers caution that there were fewer participants involved in this study than initially expected, which may jeopardize their results.
The study was conducted in South Africa.
It supports a program to conduct trials to assess whether it is appropriate to administer high doses of rifampicin to HIV patients with tuberculosis meningitis.
It is hoped that such treatment will save more lives in Africa and other parts of the world where meningitis is a major problem.
Can the incorporation of a mixture of compost and biochar improve the quality of eroded savanna soil along the coast?
The decline in soil fertility is a major challenge in crop production in sub-Saharan Africa.
The positive impact of the incorporation of biochar and compost on soil fertility has been reported by many authors.

In this study, a 30-day laboratory incubation was analyzed using 120 g samples of Haplic acrisol mixed with biochar from maize cobs (cbio), rice husk biochar (rbio), coconut husk biochar (coco300 and coco700), or chicken manure (compost); and rice husk biochar compost (rcocomp) or maize cob biochar compost (cococomp) at an amendment rate of 1% w/w: respectively in the soil.

In another set of this study, chicken manure was combined with biochar from either wood chips or rice husks (1% compost + 1% biochar: 1% soil w/w), respectively, to assess their impact on soil respiration, soil pH; microbial carbon in the soil; cation exchange capacity; total organic carbon; total nitrogen and the presence of available nitrogen.
Biochar and compost applied separately or together, and biochar compost increased soil pH by 0.28-2.29 pH units compared to the untreated control.
Emissions from rice husk or rice husk biochar, or biochar mixed with manure were higher than untreated ones, similar to those treated with biochar alone.
The TOC in the sole compost and in the biochar with added manure increased by 37% and 117%, respectively, compared to the untreated one.
The application of rice husk biochar mixed with manure increased the MBC by 132% while manure alone increased the MBC by 247%, respectively, compared to the untreated soil.

In conclusion, the study demonstrated that the application of manure alone or mixed with biochar, or biochar manure improves soil parameter levels such as soil pH and MBC, and also promotes soil C stability by increasing TOC and reducing soil C loss through respiration.
Biochar and compost improve the quality of soil for planting.
This study investigates how biochar, a highly stable ash with high carbon content, derived from waste biomass, can be used to improve the quality of soils in sub-Saharan Africa.
The study found that biochar improves soil quality in a manner similar to other expensive and less accessible methods.
One of the major challenges facing crop production in sub-Saharan Africa is the decline in soil fertility.
Better soil leads to better yields, which can reduce hunger in rural areas and restore natural resources in the area.

Point-of-Care (POC) testing in communities, home settings, and primary healthcare facilities is believed to have great potential in reducing delays in the diagnosis and initiation of treatment for diseases such as HIV, tuberculosis, gonorrhea, and malaria.

However, the availability of inexpensive, simple, and rapid tests that can be conducted outside of laboratories does not automatically guarantee effective POC testing.

To understand the new roles and challenges of medical tools such as this integration, we need to research how diagnostics are used at the point of care (POC) and integrated into the workflow and patient pathways.
This chapter reviews selected findings from a high-level research project on barriers to POC testing in India and South Africa and discusses them comparatively.

The project utilized unstructured interviews and focus group discussions to assess diagnostic approaches for all major diseases and actors in homes, clinics, communities, hospitals, and laboratories in South Africa and India.
In comparing the selected outcomes, it is clear that both countries have very different diagnostic systems that provide very different conditions for POC testing.
The chapter concludes by reflecting on how to consider such information when designing POC testing programs.
The examination of inadequate care facilities in South Africa and India delays healthcare delivery.
Point of care (POC) refers to health care testing conducted at the same location where the patient receives care, rather than sending patient samples to a laboratory for analysis.
South Africa and India do not deliver rapid and effective testing due to their poor POC systems and laboratories.
POC testing allows patients to access rapid testing with quick results for the treatment and management of diseases.
This can be done with inexpensive and simple machines that can provide test results quickly without sending samples to laboratories.
However, there are many challenges in POC that limit patient care in South Africa and India.
The authors wanted to compare POC testing in South Africa and India to identify issues.
They held discussions and meetings with health workers, patients, and medical device companies from September 2012 to June 2013 in both countries.
They asked about the procedures and issues of POC.

Researchers also noted that sometimes patients are tested but it takes a long time for the results to come back, and they find it difficult to contact their doctor afterwards.

In South Africa, they found that in public healthcare, one company is responsible for all testing, so samples go to this company.
Some basic testing is conducted at the point of care, and patients receive results quickly.

Some delays are due to transportation, incorrect spelling of patient names, incorrect labeling of samples, and computer system failures.

Researchers suggested that healthcare workers should collaborate to share the workload.
They said that when new resources for testing the HIV virus are introduced, workers must be retrained and the programs must be adjusted.
The authors compared the POC contribution from both countries and suggested that authorities should carefully consider the POC before adding new products or devices.

Regarding the definitions of critical illness and critical care using conceptual analysis

As "serious illness" and "critical care" lack consensus definitions, this study aims to explore how these concepts are used, describe their defining characteristics, and propose potential definitions.
We used the Walker and Avant method for concept analysis.
The use and definitions of concepts were identified through a scoping review of the literature and an online survey of 114 global clinical experts.
By analyzing the content of the data, we extracted codes, categories, and themes to determine the attributes that define concepts and suggest possible interpretations.
To aid understanding, we presented models, related and opposing cases about concepts, identified antecedents and outcomes in concepts, and explained strong references.
The defining characteristics of severe illness were a significant risk of imminent death; dysfunction of vital organs; the need for care to avoid death; and potential deterioration.

The features of critical care were the identification, monitoring, and treatment of critical illnesses; support of vital organs; initial and ongoing care; any care for a critical illness; and specialized resources for individuals and the body.
Our proposed definition of critical illness states, "a condition of significant dysfunction in a vital organ, a high risk of imminent death if care is not provided, and the potential for recovery."
Our proposed definition of critical care is, "the identification, monitoring, and treatment of patients with severe illness by providing initial and ongoing support for vital organ functions."
The signs of critical illness and critical care do not have consistent definitions and have various applications.

Through the analysis of the concept of usage and definitions in literature and among experts, we identified descriptive attributes of concepts and proposed definitions that could aid clinical practice, research, and policy-making.
The Power and Limitations of the Study
This conceptual analysis is the first study to systematically describe the use and definitions of concepts of critical illness and critical care.

The study utilizes a scoping review of the literature and inputs from over a hundred clinical experts from different parts of the world to identify descriptive attributes and provide proposed definitions of concepts.
Other uses and definitions of concepts in languages other than English, in unpublished grey literature and health experts not included in the study may be missed.
As the current use of concepts varies, the proposed definitions may not be universally accepted and are intended to provoke further discussion.
Researchers also described the definition of "critically ill" patients and their care.
The common patient care guidelines used worldwide by all doctors can assist in the care of critically ill patients.
In this study, the international team of researchers suggests that "severe disease" should mean that although the patient has a high risk of death, they may recover.
They further stated that the "care" provided to critically ill patients should mean any care given from the time they arrive at the hospital until they either pass away or recover.
It should also be referred to care using specialized equipment.
In hospitals, doctors often refer to very ill patients as "critically ill", and the care and support required by these patients is called "critical care".
However, doctors working in different regions or hospitals understand these terms differently, because their definitions vary from one place to another.
This causes, for example, patients with the same condition to receive different treatment or care, depending on who is assisting them.
Different interpretations also make it difficult for governments to know the true number of serious diseases in their country.
In this study, researchers first analyzed how different doctors describe "serious illness" and "critical care," then proposed standardized definitions.
They gather information by reviewing certain published articles.
They also consulted with doctors from several different countries around the world who have experience in treating critically ill patients.

Researchers wrote different descriptions of critical illnesses, and noted that they were generally associated with a higher risk of patient mortality; dysfunction of some body organs; the need for care to avoid death; and the chance of recovery.

In the matter of death and recovery, some interpretations suggested that all critically ill patients would eventually die, while others indicated the possibility of a patient recovering despite being critically ill.

Ultimately, researchers suggested that severe illness be defined as an illness where organ systems fail, where there is a high likelihood of patient death if not properly cared for, but with a chance of recovery.
With critical care, doctors seem to describe it in a similar way, but differ on where such care should be provided, and the need for specialized equipment.
Some sources stated that critical care can only be provided in certain specialized areas of a hospital with specialized equipment.
Some felt that critical care might involve using specialized resources, but it was not a requirement.
They said that critical care can be provided even in regular wards, in small health facilities, in the community, or in ambulances.
Even in the poorest areas, critically ill patients require intensive care.

Therefore, researchers suggest that critical care can be defined as all the care that severely ill patients receive from the time they visit healthcare workers for consultation until they either recover or pass away.

Researchers stated that this is the first study to gather information on different definitions of illness and critical care, and they said their results will help improve the care of severely ill patients.
However, they state that their study may have limitations because they did not use definitions from languages other than English or from unpublished sources.
They also consulted with doctors from only a few countries, so their analysis does not represent all countries in the world.
Researchers from universities in Malawi, Tanzania, Sweden, and the UK stated that their proposed explanations can be adjusted if necessary.

In this chapter, we examine the extent of research in South Africa focused on biological invasions compared to other aspects of global change.

Using the Web of Science, we systematically reviewed literature related to the South African environment published between 2000 and 2018 and concerning biological invasions, climate change, overharvesting, habitat transformation, land pollution, and/or atmospheric CO2.
We identified 1149 relevant papers that were scored based on their driver cover and driver interactions affecting biodiversity or ecosystem services.
A strong spatio-temporal effect was observed in the research effort.

Firstly, efforts varied across regions, where habitat alteration, land pollution, and overharvesting received research that was highly focused on terrestrial, freshwater, and marine/riverine areas respectively.
Secondly, certain well-studied phenomena worldwide are not documented in local literature (e.g., there were fewer than five papers on ocean acidification).
We identified 21 different interactions among drivers, and the interaction between invasive species and land-use change (for example, altered fire regimes in invaded areas) is particularly prominent.
However, less than 4% of the papers discussed interactions among three or more drivers.

This suggests that although the importance of understanding driver interactions is recognized, there has been little research into the combined effects of driver interactions in the ecosystems of South Africa.

The previously quoted statement that invasive species are the second largest threat to biodiversity conservation, after habitat change, aligns with the findings of research related to this driver in South Africa.

Developing a comprehensive picture of the relative importance of global change drivers will be challenging, not only in clearly defining the drivers, but also due to the availability of uneven research outcomes on a comparable spatial and temporal scale.
The controlled maturation of invasive species activity may provide a basis for examining such complex interactions and thus contribute to overcoming those barriers.
Researchers must map the combined effects of invasive species, climate change, and human activities in South Africa.

Female genital mutilation/cutting is a harmful traditional practice that violates women's rights and has adverse health consequences.
This paper presents the reasons and circumstances for the determination/cutting (FGM/C) in certain areas of three countries - Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.

Data was collected through a household survey involving young people (aged 15-24) and through focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, and key informant interviews with youth and community stakeholders in 2016 and 2017.
Descriptive statistics and content analysis of the corpus were conducted.
The results of the study confirm some of the reasons for FGM/C documented in previous research, noting that these reasons are highly interconnected, and gender norms are the main cause.
In all three of these settings, these reasons drive the transformation of women's bodies to produce a 'culturally enhanced' body that is acceptable in the ancestral context.
This results in a 'clean body' in Indonesia, a 'soft body' in Ethiopia, and an 'adult body' in Kenya.
Health workers and parents play a crucial role in decision-making regarding FGM/C in all contexts.
In Kenya, in particular, young women discuss their role in decision-making regarding FGM/C as they have matured at the time of circumcision.

The study reveals how changes in legal and social conditions in each area have brought about transformations in the practice of FGM/C, leading to the medicalization of FGM/C in Indonesia, a decrease in the age of cutting for girls in Kenya, and an increasing underground practice of FGM/C in Ethiopia.
These three scenarios demonstrate significant variation in the practice of FGM/C and the social meaning associated with it by young women and their communities.
There is a need to continue analyzing the role of parents in decision-making.

Due to the interaction between different drivers of FGM/C within each context, the study concludes that context-specific strategies need to be adopted in a targeted manner to effect long-lasting change.
To stop female genital mutilation, we first need to understand why it happens.
Female genital mutilation, a practice where parts of female genital organs are cut or removed, occurs illegally or secretly in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
Researchers say that understanding why it happens is key to stopping this harmful practice, and preventing the health and mental issues that women face as a result.
In certain parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), sometimes referred to as 'female circumcision', is still commonly practiced.
Many people falsely believe that FGM is necessary for proper hygiene or to keep women modest (not promiscuous and submissive), and they are convinced that it will ensure they can have children.
FGM is not required for any of these according to scientific evidence.
In many cases, however, children who undergo FGM end up with health problems later in life, such as dangerous infections, difficulty urinating (straining), and mental health issues.
Because this practice is dangerous and violates women's rights, many countries have made it illegal, but people still do it secretly.
In this study, researchers aimed to gain a deeper understanding of why FGM occurs in different countries, and what people believe about this practice.
Therefore, they collect information about FGM in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
In each country, researchers spoke to people about this practice, including parents, youth, traditional leaders, health workers, and 'cutters' (older women who used to perform FGM on young girls).
In some cases, they engaged with these individuals individually, but they also spoke to groups of people, including young adults and youth, who have been affected by FGM.
Researchers found that the reasons for FGM, the way it is performed, and beliefs about the practice, differ in each country.
They also found that many people still perform them even in places where it is illegal.
For example, in Indonesia, traditional midwives used a knife or needle to cut part of the clitoris (the main organ responsible for sexual pleasure in women) when a baby girl was 40 days old.
People believed that this helps in 'removing impurities' and that it was important for religious reasons.
In Ethiopia, FGM occurred even before that, sometimes when children were only 7 days old.
Researchers found that the local people believed that this would ensure that the girl would become a 'good wife' one day, and that she would be obedient and not violent towards her husband.
Many people believe that FGM makes childbirth easier but in fact, it can make giving birth much more difficult.
During that time in Kenya, FGM indicated that a girl had reached womanhood, and it often occurred later in life, when she was a teenager.

In some cases, however, they found that girls could undergo FGM as young as 8 years old, and that many girls ended up pregnant at a young age, because they were considered mature enough for sexual activity after FGM.
Researchers say their findings indicate that there are many reasons why it occurs.
As social norms and ideas change, how and where things are done also changes.
For example, parents may attempt to do it secretly even though it is illegal, because they believe it is necessary for their daughter to have good health or to find a good husband.
It is important to recognize that because FGM is illegal in some areas, researching the topic can be difficult, and people may not always provide truthful responses about the subject.

In the future, in addition to legalizing, researchers say governments and health authorities should aim to stop FGM by addressing the false beliefs people have about the practice and educating them about the risks.

This study was a collaboration between scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and is part of a larger program called 'Yes I Do', aimed at reducing teenage pregnancies, child marriage, and FGM.

Hormonal Imbalance of Reproductive Hormones, Germ Cell Apoptosis, Abnormal Sperm Morphophenotypes and Ultra-Structural Changes in African Giant Rats (Cricetomys gaambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Toxicity
Environmental exposure to vanadium has been increasing recently.
This metal is a known poison.
The current study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in African giant rats.
The use of SMV was administered intraperitoneally daily for 14 consecutive days at a dose of 3 mg/kg body weight.
Plain water was given to the control group.
We analyzed reproductive hormones in serum, sperm retention and quality, and ultrastructural changes of the testes after SMV treatment.
Our results showed that the exposed SMV group of AGR statistically increased progesterone but decreased the concentration of testosterone, FSH, and LH.

Furthermore, the group treated with SMV showed a statistically significant decrease in sperm motility and an increase in the percentage of abnormal spermatozoa morphophenotypes and the regulation of P53 immunopositive cells.
Ultrastructural study reveals viral vacuolation and Sertoli cells, both cytoplasmic and nuclear; as well as mitochondrial swelling and vacuole extrusion were also observed.
There was significant disintegration of seminiferous tubules, atrophy and degeneration of myeloid cells, and apoptosis of Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells.

In conclusion, intraperitoneal exposure to SMV has very adverse effects on some reproductive hormones in the serum, reducing sperm storage and quality, apoptosis, and degenerative changes in Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells which can lead to infertility.
Researchers say that the metal found in polluted air causes mice to become infertile.
Researchers found that vanadium, a type of metal, damages mouse cells and their ability to reproduce (fertility).

Because this metal is also toxic to humans, they recommend further research to determine whether the metal, increasingly found in the environment due to pollution, could have similar adverse effects on human health.
Even though vanadium is a metal, it can enter the air in small amounts when fuels, such as oil and coal, are burned.
As the world consumes more of these fossil fuel resources, the amount of vanadium pollution is increasing.
We already know that people exposed to it may experience health issues such as anemia, dry throat and eyes, and chest pain.
Recently, scientists have become interested in the potential effects vanadium may have on reproduction.
They have started studying these results in mice, which are commonly used in laboratories due to their similarity to humans.
In this study, scientists were interested in the effects of vanadium on a common species of rat found in West Africa, known as the African Giant Rat.
They wanted to understand how vanadium affects the reproductive systems of male mice, particularly their sperm, hormones, and testicular cells.
Researchers injected 6 male mice with vanadium once a day, for 14 days.
At the same time, they injected another 6 mice with water as a "control" test.
Because the water will not affect the mice, researchers can be sure that any changes they observe in the first six mice are the result of the vanadium injections.
After 14 days, they checked whether the levels of hormones like testosterone had changed, then examined the testes and counted their sperm.
Using a method called Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), they were able to observe any changes occurring in the testes in detail, down to the level of individual cells.
Researchers found that mice injected with vanadium had significantly lower levels of testosterone, and other hormones important for reproduction.
Mice injected with Vanadium also had significantly reduced sperm, and their sperm had a shorter lifespan.
Researchers observed, for example, that some mouse sperm were headless or had a bent tail, and that they were not as motile as sperm from mice injected with water.
Because sperm are the male reproductive cells of living organisms, used to fertilize eggs in females, these changes can make it very difficult for mice to reproduce successfully.
Finally, researchers found that some cells from the testes of mice were severely damaged or destroyed by vanadium.
Researchers stated that the changes they found could eventually lead to infertility.
They noted that as animals exposed to vanadium and other pollutants in the surrounding environment may be unable to reproduce, they could potentially become extinct due to these effects.
Because humans are mammals like rats, scientists must also study any potential negative effects of vanadium in polluted areas on human health.

Researchers have warned that some of the changes they found in the anatomy and hormones of animals were different from what previous scientific studies found, therefore additional work is needed to understand the damage caused by vanadium.
This study was a collaboration between scientists from Nigeria and Egypt, and it adds to what scientists know about how animals, and possibly humans, are affected by pollution.
The Traditional Use of Indigenous Plants in the Indigenous Community of Northwest Ethiopia
The composition of flowers in homegardens in Northwestern Ethiopia in general, and the Gozamin district in particular, has received little research attention.
The aim of this study is to better understand the composition of plants and the cultural significance of homegardens.
A stratified random sampling procedure was used based on agroecological variations in the selected kebeles.

The homegarden data was collected by dividing the homegarden into four quadrats, the first quadrat extending from the farmer's house to 10m, the second quadrat from 10m to 20m, the third from 20m to 30m, and the fourth quadrat from 30m to 40m horizontally as the axis depending on the size of the garden.
A semi-structured interview was conducted to document the knowledge of an individual with expertise in plant species.
A total of 238 culturally significant plant species from 81 families have been identified.
Of these, 39% were herbs, 29% were trees, and 6% were climbers.
Perennial plants constitute a large portion of the cultivated species (83%), while annuals make up the remainder (17%).
The Poaceae family had the most leading species, with 22, followed by Fabaceae, which had 21, and Asteraceae, which had 15.

Of the recorded plants, 140 (58.6%) were species used for natural use, 84 (35%) were food plants, 83 (34.7%) were medicinal plant species, 39 (16.3%) were polish species, 57 (23.8%) were plants, 60 (25%) were wood species, 50 (21%) were plants used by the community, and 1 (0.4%) was poisonous.
The direct matrix ranking revealed that Cordia Africana was identified as a multifunctional plant important for cultural practices in the area and was also at high risk, followed by Ficus sur.
The highest number of Cordia africana used was for construction and the list value was for medicinal purposes.
The Sorensen similarity index of 64% of the investigated sites was below 0.5.
The result showed that homegardens have multiple functions, long-term production systems.
The security of food and the conservation of biodiversity are continuously supported by the cultural knowledge of indigenous peoples related to their animals.
Low similarity/high diversity of species in the area among kebeles indicated that there was a high species diversity due to the distinct range of agroecological conditions among the kebeles.
Ethiopian gardens support food security and conservation.
Researchers say that many people in Ethiopia cultivate food, ornamental plants, medicinal plants, and plants for feeding animals, shade, or fencing in their gardens.
They have examined these gardens to see how important they are in ensuring food availability and helping with environmental conservation.
Communities around the world maintain gardens for food, to make money, and for other cultural purposes.
Gardens also protect important plants that are often absent or disappear in other areas.
In Ethiopia, there is not much research conducted regarding what communities plant in their gardens.
In this study, researchers aimed to investigate the plants that people in the Gozamin district, in Northwestern Ethiopia, cultivate in their gardens and what they use them for.
They identified and counted 357 plants in the area.
They also engaged with the community about how they use the plants.
Researchers found that all gardens in Gozamin were less than a hectare in size.
They collected and identified 238 different plant species.
Many plants (83%) were cultivated year-round, and only a few (17%) had specific seasonal periods.
Their results showed that the community used plants for food, medicine, building, fodder (animal feed), and other cultural uses.
Many plants serve more than one purpose.
For example, the Northern tree with large leaves can be used for medicine, decoration, polish, shade, fencing, and other cultural uses.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for environmental purposes such as fencing, hedging, shading, and decoration.
Researchers said this helps protect the environment.
Fencing crops also helped in protecting farm produce.
More than one-third (35%) of the crops were harvested for consumption, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and spices.
However, they said that the gardens in this area mainly provide fruits.

Researchers stated that 35% of the plants were used as traditional medicine for the well-being of animals and livestock, while 21% were used for religious practices and purposes, smoking, perfumes, and baking.
Some plants (17%) were used as fodder to feed cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
Some (24%) work as materials for construction, making garden tools, thatching with grass, and making ropes.
As most rural people are reported to use wood, 25% of plants are used for that purpose.
Researchers stated that only one plant (0.4%) was mentioned with the intention of poisoning.
They also stated that the way plants are distributed in an area is influenced by the environment, people's preferences, and the family's financial situation and business needs.
For example, the area called Wenka, which had irrigation water and was near a large city, had many gardens and recorded 130 different plant species.
The people of Wenka also cultivated and brought fruits and vegetables to the city market.
Finally, researchers say that most farmers prefer to grow crops that are widely used.
Researchers stated that their results confirm that indeed farmers grow a large number of different types of crops in their gardens, as well as diverse uses.
Although these researchers found that many farmers plant herbs, some researchers say that trees are more common in the area.
The researchers of this study were based at universities in Ethiopia.
